sentences.sentence: Pronunciation: tur-ZEP-uh-tide Brand names: Zepbound , Zepbound KwikPen, Mounjaro , Mounjaro KwikPen Dosage form: Subcutaneous injection Drug class: GLP-1 Drugs
Medically reviewed by Melisa Puckey, BPharm .
Last updated on Sep 30, 2026.

Tirzepatide is a once-weekly injection available as two brands: Zepbound (for weight loss, weight management, and obstructive sleep apnea) and Mounjaro (for type 2 diabetes and to lower the risk of major adverse cardiovascular events in those with type 2 diabetes at high risk).
Zepbound (tirzepatide) is FDA-approved for weight loss and weight management in adults with obesity, or in overweight adults with at least one weight-related medical condition.
Zepbound is also approved to treat moderate-to-severe obstructive sleep apnea (OSA) in adults with obesity.
Mounjaro (tirzepatide) is FDA-approved for type 2 diabetes in adults and children aged 10 years and older to help improve blood sugar (glucose) levels, used alongside diet and exercise.

It is also approved to lower the risk of major adverse cardiovascular events (cardiovascular death, non-fatal heart attack, or non-fatal stroke) in adults with type 2 diabetes who are at high risk for these events.
Tirzepatide is a dual GIP/ GLP-1 receptor agonist , meaning it activates two gut hormone receptors that help regulate appetite, digestion, and blood sugar.
It works by reducing appetite, increasing feelings of fullness, slowing gastric emptying, boosting insulin release when blood sugar is high, and reducing glucagon secretion.
Tirzepatide is self-administered as a subcutaneous (under the skin) injection using a single-dose pen, KwikPen, or vial with syringe, and should always be used together with diet and exercise.
Tirzepatide should not be used in people with type 1 diabetes.
It is not known if tirzepatide is safe in people who have had pancreatitis.

The most common tirzepatide side effects are:
Diarrhea
Vomiting
Constipation
Nausea (mild to moderate)
Decreased appetite
Abdominal pain.
Tirzepatide can cause serious side effects.
Call your doctor right away if you have any of the following:

Severe stomach pain (pancreatitis): Stop taking tirzepatide and call your healthcare provider immediately if you have severe pain in your stomach area that will not go away, with or without vomiting, or pain that spreads to your back.
Kidney problems: Diarrhea, nausea, and vomiting can cause dehydration, which may lead to kidney problems.
Drink plenty of fluids to reduce this risk and tell your doctor if you are unable to keep fluids down.
Gallbladder problems: Symptoms include severe upper stomach pain, fever, nausea, vomiting, yellowing of the skin or eyes (jaundice), or clay-colored stools.

Serious allergic reactions: Seek emergency medical attention if you experience hives, difficulty breathing, feeling light-headed, or swelling of your face, lips, tongue, or throat (anaphylaxis or angioedema).
Low blood sugar (hypoglycemia): Symptoms may include headache, hunger, weakness, sweating, confusion, irritability, dizziness, fast heart rate, or feeling jittery.
Vision changes: Tell your doctor about any blurred vision or other vision changes, particularly if you have type 2 diabetes.
Thyroid tumor: Symptoms may include a lump or swelling in your neck, trouble swallowing, hoarseness, or shortness of breath.
Mental health changes: Tell your healthcare provider right away about any new or worsening depression, mood changes, or thoughts of suicide or self-harm.
Aspiration during surgery: Tirzepatide slows stomach emptying, which may increase the risk of food or liquid entering the lungs during procedures using anesthesia or sedation.
Tell all your healthcare providers you are taking tirzepatide before any planned surgery or procedure.
This is not a complete list of side effects.
Call your doctor for medical advice about side effects, or report them to the FDA at 1-800-FDA-1088.
Who should not use tirzepatide:
Type 1 diabetes patients (tirzepatide is not approved for type 1 diabetes)
Personal or family history of medullary thyroid carcinoma (MTC)
Multiple Endocrine Neoplasia syndrome type 2 (MEN 2).
Use with Caution:
History of pancreatitis (safety not established in patients with prior pancreatitis)
Severe gastrointestinal disease
Diabetic retinopathy complications.
Tirzepatide carries a Boxed Warning for the risk of possible thyroid tumors.
Tell your healthcare provider if you get a lump or swelling in your neck, hoarseness, trouble swallowing, or shortness of breath.
These may be symptoms of thyroid cancer.
In studies with rats, tirzepatide and medicines that work like tirzepatide have caused thyroid tumors, including thyroid cancer.
It is not known if tirzepatide will cause thyroid tumors, or a type of thyroid cancer called medullary thyroid carcinoma (MTC) in people.

Do not use tirzepatide if you or any of your family have ever had a type of thyroid cancer called medullary thyroid carcinoma (MTC), or if you have an endocrine system condition called Multiple Endocrine Neoplasia syndrome type 2 (MEN 2).
Tell your doctor and pharmacist if you are allergic to tirzepatide, any other medications, or any of the ingredients in this medicine.
There is a list of ingredients in this medicine, at the bottom of this page.
Tell your healthcare team if you are planning surgery or other procedure that uses anesthesia or deep sedation.
Tell your doctor if you have or have ever had kidney or pancreas disease, a history of diabetic retinopathy or any stomach problems such as difficulty digesting food.
Tell your doctor if you plan to become pregnant, are pregnant, or are breastfeeding.
If you become pregnant while taking this medicine, you should tell your doctor.
There is a pregnancy exposure registry for women who take Zepbound during pregnancy.
Talk to your healthcare provider about how you can take part, call 1-844-524-0039, or visit https://pregnancyregistry.lilly.com/zepbound.

You should follow the directions on your prescription label carefully and ask your pharmacist or doctor to explain any part you do not understand.
It is important to use this medicine exactly as directed.
Do not take more or less of it or take it more often than prescribed by your doctor.
Tirzepatide is injected under the skin (subcutaneously) using a pre-filled single-dose pen, a multi-dose KwikPen (for single patient use), and a single-dose vial with a syringe.
Caregivers or patients should be trained on proper injection techniques and should read the instructions for use .
Children should not inject themselves with the KwikPen; an adult caregiver should give a child their injections.
Tirzepatide is usually given:
once a week.
can be given with or without meals at any time of the day.
may be injected into the thigh, abdomen, or have another person inject it into the back of your upper arm
You should rotate injection sites with each dose.
Do not inject into a muscle (intramuscularly) or vein (intravenously).
Do not mix insulin and tirzepatide together in the same injection.
You may give an injection of tirzepatide and insulin in the same body area, but not right next to each other.
Your doctor will probably start you on a low dose, which may be gradually increased, but not more than once every 4 weeks.
You may change the day of the week you use tirzepatide as long as there are at least three days between doses.
Do not stop taking this medicine without talking to your doctor.
The KwikPen contains 4 fixed doses, and one dose is injected weekly (subcutaneously).
For your weekly dose, you need to turn the dose knob all the way until it stops AND the 1 icon is in the dose window.
After 4 doses, throw away (discard) the Pen, including the unused medicine.
The Pen will prevent you from dialing a full dose after you have given yourself 4 weekly doses.
Do not inject the leftover medicine.
Do not transfer the leftover medicine from your Pen into a syringe.
Do not share your tirzepatide Pen with other people, even if the pen needle has been changed.
You may give other people a serious infection or get a serious infection from them.
People who are blind or have vision problems should not use the Pen without help from a person who has been trained to use the pen.

Single-dose pens and vials (Zepbound and Mounjaro)
Store in the refrigerator between 36°F and 46°F (2°C and 8°C).
Do not freeze.
Do not use if the medication has been frozen.
Keep in the original carton until use to protect from light.
If needed, single-dose pens and vials may be kept at room temperature up to 86°F (30°C) for up to 21 days.
Once at room temperature, do not return to the refrigerator.
Discard after 21 days at room temperature if unused.
KwikPen (Zepbound KwikPen and Mounjaro KwikPen)
Before first use:
Store in the refrigerator between 36°F and 46°F (2°C and 8°C).
Keep until the expiration date printed on the label.
Do not freeze.
Discard the pen if it has been frozen.
After first use:
Store in the refrigerator or at room temperature up to 86°F (30°C).
Keep away from heat and light.
Discard the pen 30 days after first use, even if medicine remains.
Discard after 4 weekly doses have been given.
General storage advice (all tirzepatide products)
Keep all pens, vials, needles, and syringes out of reach of children.
Dispose of used pens, needles, and syringes in an approved sharps container.

The most effective GLP-1 drug for weight loss currently (as of early 2026) is tirzepatide, marketed under the names Zepbound (for weight loss) and Mounjaro (for diabetes).
Clinical trials and recent meta-analyses consistently show tirzepatide delivers the most substantial weight reduction among GLP-1 medications, with average losses of up to 22.5% of body weight.

Mounjaro (generic name: tirzepatide) will start to lower your blood sugar levels right away but it can take 8 to 12 weeks to reach your target A1C goal.
When compared to some other diabetes treatments, studies have shown that it can take 8 weeks to reach an A1C target of ≤7% and 12 weeks to reach an A1C ≤6.5% with Mounjaro.
Significant weight loss can occur as early as 28-weeks.

Semaglutide and tirzepatide are prescription medicines used for type 2 diabetes and long-term weight management.
Semaglutide products include Ozempic, Rybelsus, Wegovy, and Wegovy HD, while tirzepatide products include Mounjaro and Zepbound.
These medicines differ in dosing, approved uses, side effects, and cost, so discuss options with your healthcare provider.
